Dear Mailing List Users,

I have a question to which I couldn't find a solution myself despite hours
of googling, or better said I am not sure. I am trying to model a network
via an ERGM. There is one node-set reflecting agents which close undirected
ties at multiple occasions/settings. These occasions/settings can be
categorized in let's say five categories. For each edge falling in each
category I have a number indicating how often this connection occurred. So
the edge list looks something like this (h head, t tail, v value, s
setting):

h t  v s
1 2 5 cat1
3 4 9 cat2
4 6 3 cat1

Since I have connection counts I am going to use "ergm.count" with
different parameters as sum, nodematch, nodemix etc. But, how can measure
which influence the setting has on the tie formation process? Ideally I
would like to get all the coefficients for each setting in one estimation
since these networks are not independent from each other. Most of the
agents interact in each section but possibly in different manners.

I looked at various options from information pieces I found on this mailing
list and elsewhere, but I am not sure which one is the one I would need:

- meta analysis: this sounds the most promising to be honest but seems not
very sophisticated (it doesn't have to be sophisticated but it should be
methodologically solid)
- multilevel ergms: this is not supported by the statnet packages so I
followed the advice which I found somewhere to use MPNet. It however only
supports two levels.
- hergm: seems to try to estimate the blocks/clusters/settings from within
the data, but my settings are given
- blockmodelling e.g. with pajek: supports multilevel models but doesn't
allow me to estimate things like node mix coefficients
- I found some infos about modeling multimode (two-mode) networks with ergm
but this doesn't seem to apply to my situation because my node set cannot
be partioned, everybody appears in every setting if even in different ways.
- somewhere here on the mailing list a user mentioned that one could
circumvent the lack of the possibility of estimating multilevel ergms by
diagonal block adjacency matrices. Unfortunately he din't outline how this
works in detail and I couldn't find more information about that.

I would be really grateful if somebody could give me a hint! It doesn't
have o be a full out line, sometimes only a keyword is enough so that I
know what I have to look for. Thanks in advance!

Best,

Andreas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andreas,

It sounds like you are looking for a combination of a valued ERGM (e.g., 
via ergm.count or GERGM) and a multiplex ERGM. As far as I know, that 
combination does not exist yet. To explore how each of the settings 
works (as a second-best solution), you can try to model each of them 
separately for now and include (functions of) the other settings as 
covariates.

Note: there is quite some confusion over terminology. Some people call 
multiplex ERGMs multi-level ERGMs while others reserve that term for 
things like social-ecological networks where you have multiple node sets 
AND within- and between-set relations. In some parts of the literature 
(mainly the hard sciences), you can also find the term 'multilayer 
networks'.

Best,
Philip

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shupin,
  I can't speak well about the appropriateness of the model, but from a 
data handling perspective I think you would need to use a term like 
'edgecov' or 'dyadcov' that accepts a matrix of dyadic covariates.  This 
would allow you to have time1 values corresponding to both edges that 
exist and don't exist in time2.  However, you will need to make the 
networks comparable, either by sub-setting both networks to only include 
the vertices present in both (perhaps using get.inducedSubgraph) or 
using xergm's adjust() function as Phillip suggests to scale the t1 
matrix according to the matrix labels in t1 and t2 -- although this will 
require introducing missing data.

If you definitely want to apply the t1 edge attributes to t2 edges, you 
need to be very careful when mapping edge attributes from one network to 
another using %e% to ensure that you are using a matrix of edge values 
and not the vector of values ordered by an arbitrary edgeId. Otherwise 
there is no guarantee that they would get applied to the same dyads. 
You would still need to transform the t1 matrix to match the t2 network, 
but the t1 values corresponding to edges that don't exist in t2 would 
not get recorded since there is no edge to attach them to.

Here is a toy example:

library(network)
t1<-network.initialize(3)
# label the vertices
network.vertex.names(t1)<-c("a","b","c")
# add some edges
t1[1,2]<-1  # 'a-b edge'
t1[2,3]<-1  # 'b-c edge'
# add an attribute
t1%e%'value'<-7

# peek at the matrix
# need to tell it attrname to fill in
as.matrix(t1,attrname='value')

   a b c
a 0 7 0
b 0 0 7
c 0 0 0


t2<-network.initialize(4)
# vertex set will partially overlap with t1
network.vertex.names(t2)<-c("b","c","d","e")
# remember that vertex '1' in t1 is not the same as '1' in t2!
t2[1,2]<-1  # the 'b-c' edge still exists
t2[2,3]<-1  # there is a new 'c-d' edge
as.matrix(t2)

   b c d e
b 0 1 0 0
c 0 0 1 0
d 0 0 0 0
e 0 0 0 0

# do this:
library(xergm.common)
# construct the matrix of t1 values for vertices
# that appear in t2 and fill in NA for missing vertices
t1val<-adjust(as.matrix(t1,attrname = 'value'),t2)
t1val # peek at matrix, notice NAs

    b  c  d  e
b  0  7 NA NA
c  0  0 NA NA
d NA NA NA NA
e NA NA NA NA


# assign the matrix
t2%e%'value'<-t1val
as.matrix(t2,attrname='value')
# notice that the 'b-c' edge took the value 7,
# but the 'c-d' edge is now NA

   b c  d e
b 0 7  0 0
c 0 0 NA 0
d 0 0  0 0
e 0 0  0 0

# DON"T DO THIS:
# tries to break the network object up
# and attach parts of it to random edges (ouch!)
# and so gives error
t2%e%'value'<-t1

# DON'T DO THIS:
# gives error t1 matrix is not same size as t2
t2%e%'value'<-as.matrix(t1)

# THIS WILL SHOOT YOU IN THE FOOT:
# the two edge values from t2 will get applied to the
# two edges in t2, BUT TO THE WRONG EDGES
t2%e%'value'<-t1%e%'value'


If you were working with a longer network time series, I would recommend 
using the networkDynamic package and dynamic network attributes and 
persistent ids as a data model keep everything organized -- but it may 
not be worth the trouble for two time steps.

Hope I didn't just make things more confusing

best,
  -skye

Hi Andreas,

Yes, via edgecov terms. Alternatively, you may theorize about how a 
closure of a tie in the respective network/setting is influenced by 
endogenous properties of the other settings. That is, you could include 
functions of the other network relations other than edgecov terms. For 
example, it may or may not make sense if A and B as well as B and C are 
connected in network relation 1 that this has an impact on A and C being 
connected in the other network relation. In this case, you would create 
a covariate matrix where a value of 1 between A and C indicates that 
there was a two-path between A and C in the other relation. Not sure how 
something like this would translate into a valued network context, but 
that is ultimately a matter of theory building. This is kind of the same 
logic as in a multilevel/multiplex/multirelational ERGM, except that you 
are going to estimate separate ERGMs for each relation because a 
combination of muliplex and valued ERGMs does not exist yet (which is to 
say that this would be more adequate, but it's not doable at this point, 
at least as far as I know). Not sure what your "meta analysis" 
suggestion is about.

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Coefficients of determination for ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick (and others),

I'm opening this up to the rest of the statnet_help list, as I think it's 
worth a larger discussion.  I see you also posted on SOCNET and have 
gotten some answers, so will address other issues here.

This is a good set of questions, and I don't have a packaged answer for 
you.  But on a cautionary note I would suggest that the coef of 
determination is probably a bit less straightforward in the network 
setting than it is in the LM/GLM world, at least for models with 
dyad-dependent terms.

I say this for two reasons.

First, these are models with potentially highly non-linear behaviors, 
since the dyadic-dependent terms can induce behaviors with sharp 
thresholds.  What this means is that a small change in the value of a coef 
for a dyadic-dependent term can have a very large impact on the structure 
of a network -- a much greater effect than a coef for a dyad independent 
term.  Comparing them, even if you standardize wrt the s.e.'s, raises 
substantive issues that just don't come up in the world of LMs/GLMs for 
independent data.

Second, in network models, the predictors are always correlated, and often 
highly correlated.  A classic example is triangle-based terms and isolates 
in sparse network:  for any fixed network, an increase in triangles will 
also produce more isolates (as the tie to complete a triangle is typically 
taken from an isolated dyad).  Under these conditions, it becomes 
difficult to specify the unique effect of a single term.  While this 
correlation is mechanically driven in the network context, correlated 
predictors also exist in the LM/GLM setting, but I think people often do 
not appreciate the implications (how many of us are familiar with the 6 
different types of SSQs proposed for this?).

Other than this, it's worth noting that we don't have a universally agreed 
to version of R^2 for plain-old GLMs, so we can expect some of those 
issues to propagate to ERGMs also.

Look forward to hearing from others.

best,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody. That's an interesting discussion. Here is my take:

In a GLM with independent observations, the number of observation is 
straightforward. In an ERGM, there is an issue of "data multiplication" 
because oftentimes few nodes and their decisions are responsible for 
many dyads. E.g., in a school class with 20 pupils, only 20 individuals 
collectively shape the network composed of 380 dyads, so there are 
clearly fewer than 380 independent observations, but certainly more than 
only 20, but we cannot figure out the true value. So any measure that 
has the number of observations in its definition (including R-squared) 
must be biased in a network setting with dyadic dependence.

That said, if this is just about quantifying fit in absolute terms and 
assessing the relative contribution of a single model term to that fit, 
here is a more constructive suggestion: You could try the following 
procedure as a second-best choice:

1) Estimate an ERGM.
2) Simulate many networks from it.
3) Compute the precision-recall (PR) curve.
4) Compute the area under the curve (AUC).
5) Re-estimate the model and leave out one parameter.
6) Simulate many networks from the re-estimated model.
7) Compute the PR curve also for this model/simulations.
8) Compute the AUC also for this PR curve.
9) Subtract the second from the first AUC measure, or divide the second 
by the first AUC value, or express the difference between the first and 
the second value as a share of the first value, etc.

The AUC value for the PR curve is a goodness-of-fit measure that is 
expressed in a single quantity between 0 and 1. The outcome of step 9 is 
the relative contribution of a model term to this measure.

This measure of prediction performance is not perfect because it does 
not discriminate between endogenous fit and exogenous fit. So I wouldn't 
use it to evaluate whether you did a good job of capturing network 
dependence (which is similar to AIC etc., by the way). BUT you wanted to 
express model fit in a single quantity, and this allows you to do just that.

PR-AUC is also an interesting choice because it can be used both within 
and out of sample. But don't use receiver operating characteristics (ROC 
curves) instead because that will only work well with networks with a 
density around 0.5 (but on those cases it will work well). PR focuses on 
the precision with which you predict ties, and on the recall, i.e., the 
number of ties you identified as such in the simulations.

In case you plan on using PR-AUC and related measures, you may consider 
my implementation in the xergm package. It works with ergm, btergm, 
mtergm, RSiena, and other custom network models (e.g., QAP with some 
tweaks). You can either apply it to a bunch of simulations and observed 
network(s) or you can let the gof function do all of that for you. In 
case you are interested, e-mail me and I'll send you a paper about the 
implementation and another one with an example including a stepping 
algorithm (which are both under review, so I won't just send them out to 
the whole list and have them archived...).

Take care,

Philip

> thresholds.  What this means is that a small change in the value of a
> coef for a dyadic-dependent term can have a very large impact on the
> structure of a network -- a much greater effect than a coef for a dyad
> independent term.  Comparing them, even if you standardize wrt the
> s.e.'s, raises substantive issues that just don't come up in the world
> of LMs/GLMs for independent data.
>
> Second, in network models, the predictors are always correlated, and
> often highly correlated.  A classic example is triangle-based terms and
> isolates in sparse network:  for any fixed network, an increase in
> triangles will also produce more isolates (as the tie to complete a
> triangle is typically taken from an isolated dyad).  Under these
> conditions, it becomes difficult to specify the unique effect of a
> single term.  While this correlation is mechanically driven in the
> network context, correlated predictors also exist in the LM/GLM setting,
> but I think people often do not appreciate the implications (how many of
> us are familiar with the 6 different types of SSQs proposed for this?).
>
> Other than this, it's worth noting that we don't have a universally
> agreed to version of R^2 for plain-old GLMs, so we can expect some of
> those issues to propagate to ERGMs also.
>
> Look forward to hearing from others.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jimi,
  Not sure I'm exactly understanding your question.  The timestamps can 
be any numeric value, they don't have to be integer steps. But I'm 
thinking you mean that when you watch the movie you want to see 
"3:24.05" instead of "204.05" seconds?

If so, you can do nice tricky things with the labelling by passing in an 
'xlab' (x-axis label) argument to overide the default time label created 
by render.animation().  This argument can be a special function so it 
will get updated as the movie progresses.

For example, assuming you coded the ties in seconds:

render.animation(yourMovieObject,
   xlab=function(onset){paste(onset%/%60,onset%%60,sep=":")})

should label each time slice with the minutes and seconds.  The render 
code is smart enough that if it sees that the argument is a function 
with an argument named 'onset' (or terminus, etc, see ?render.animation 
for details) it will call the function each time it plots the network, 
substituting in the current value of onset for each slice.

hope that is what you were asking :-)

best,
  -skye

messages.body_plain:
Ah, OK now I understand. That's a cool idea!  As you point out, the time 
in the input file has nothing to do with the speed/duration of the movie 
that will be created (because what if the time units were years!).   The 
speed of the movie is controlled by three things:

1) how you set the slice.par paramters to chop up your movie (i.e. 1 
network = 1 second of time, vs 5 seconds, etc)

2) How many 'in between' animation frames you tell it to render

3) How long it tries to keep each frame on screen


Assuming that you are happy with the movie are getting with your 
settings for (1), the easiest way to make your animation output go 
faster (and jerkier) or slower (and smoother) is to adjust the number of 
'in between' animation frames it renders by setting a value for the 
'tween.frames' parameter (default is 10).

render.animation(myNetwork,render.par=list(tween.frames=1))

vs

render.animation(myNetwork,render.par=list(tween.frames=30))


There is also an option provided by the animation package to set the 
duration that each frame of the animation should remain on screen. By 
default it is set to 1/10th of a second.

ani.options=list(interval=0.1)

oddly, it seems that these default settings actually *should* produce 
movies in which one time unit ~ second on screen if you have your 
slice.par set to break the network into 1 sec bins.  So I think if it 
isn't quite lining up, you may have to do some trial and error 
adjustments until you get it to sync.


BTW, dear list members, if this doesn't scare you off, we will be giving 
a workshop on ndtv and statnet's dynamic network tools at the INSNA 
conference next Tuesday evening.  Perhaps we can convince Jimi to make a 
guest appearance with this video?

best,
  -skye
